newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Belgrade bourse '96 turnover up threefold on '95.
newsitem.headline: Belgrade bourse '96 turnover up threefold on '95.

text.p: Turnover on the Belgrade Stock Exchange (BSE) rose threefold to 2.186 billion dinars ($450.7 million) in 1996 compared to 717.6 million the previous year.

"Turnover in nominal terms was three times higher than in 1995, with trade moving more and more towards state securities," BSE director Pava Zecevic told an annual meeting of the bourse Tuesday afternoon.
The National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY) bonds, first issued in November 1995 to drain liquidity from the market, accounted for 44 percent of total turnover in 1996.

Commercial paper accounted for 35 percent, followed by forward contracts selling agricultural produce as collateral issued by the Serbian Commodity Reserve Agency with 15, bank treasury bills five, and certificates of deposit one percent.
The number of transactions dropped to 7,942 from 8,252 in 1995.
The BSE's total income last year was 4.485 million dinars and profit around 22,400 dinars, Zecevic said.
Total income is expected to rise to six million dinars and expenditures to 5.9 million this year, she said.
The BSE, which celebrated its seventh anniversary last year, is impatiently expecting privatisation through which it will get more instruments to trade with.

"With the Law on Ownership Transformation, bourse trading will enter a new stage of development which should result in the forming of a capital market, vital in the privatisation process," Zecevic said.
According to Zecevic, banks were still not showing enough interest in covering the market, with only a few having their own brokers and dealers registered for trading on the bourse.
The bourse currently has 15 registered members, up from 12 last year.

"We are just on the threshold of a market economy, and this is precisely the sector on which key reforms will take place," Yugoslav Securities Commission (YSC) President Vuk Ognjanovic told the meeting.

Ognjanovic said the four major conditions for the development of the financial market are political stability and legal security, economic growth and stability, stable dinar exchange rate and interest rates.
"Of the four, only one is currently under control -- the dinar exchange rate," he said.

"We must support the creation of a strong bourse. We must not allow the BSE to go through the same adventure that our banking system went through," Ognjanovic said, referring to Yugoslavia's ailing banking sector.
He said the Yugoslav financial market lacked real secondary trading and a long-term securities market.
Another problem is that over-the-counter (OTC) trade exceeds volume of the bourse.
"OTC trade must be regulated as a trading institution with the aim of ensuring more protection for both creditors and investors," Ognjanovic said.
The current situation on the financial market is characterised by the absence of the state in trading and inadequate presence of the central bank from the discount paper market, he said.

"The BSE has made an important pioneer step and we must now exert more efforts to help strengthen the young and still green Yugoslav financial market," Ognjanovic said. -- Belgrade newsroom +381 11 222 4305 ($ = 4.85 Yugoslav Dinars)
